messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Yes. Even in these lines, Majeed’s manner remains more practical and controlling than tender. “Wake up” is abrupt, and “I am going to take both of you” sounds like an announcement, not a request, reassurance, or act of emotional tenderness. He carries Jamila, but the “thin quilt” suggests minimal, expedient covering rather than warmth or affection. Rahima is “bewildered” and follows “at his heels,” which emphasizes her dependence and his control. The “brilliant moonlight at first blinded him” can be read physically, but also symbolically: his moral or emotional sight is as impaired as his physical sight. He is not shown pausing to comfort, apologize, or acknowledge their fear. So the traits of cunning and apathy are still present, though in a quieter, more practical form.

As for motive, the lines point more strongly to a teleological than a deontological action. A deontological reading would require evidence that he saves them because it is intrinsically right, because he feels a moral duty, or because their welfare is an end in itself. That would be suggested by gentler, duty-laden language: “we must go,” “I will keep you safe,” “stay with me.” Instead, the language is goal-directed: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” The focus is on a future outcome—reaching the village, continuing the journey, avoiding danger, or preserving his plans. Even if the result is that Rahima and Jamila are saved, the motive seems instrumental: their survival is useful to him, or at least acceptable to him, rather than the point of the action. This reads as a well-calculated maneuver. It may include a small trace of protective duty, but within the excerpt and his earlier characterization, it is closer to cunning calculation than genuine deontological goodwill.
